That’s a great question. The faucet you left dripping didn’t freeze because water moving slowly through a pipe stays warmer than still water.

When water is still, it can lose heat to the cold air around it. If it’s not moving, the water in the pipe can get cold enough to freeze. But when water drips — even slowly — it moves through the pipe, and that motion helps keep the water temperature a little warmer. This is called the "drip effect."

Also, the slow flow of water keeps the pipe walls slightly moist and prevents the inside from getting too cold. So even if the outside of the pipe is freezing, the water inside (especially if it’s dripping) stays just above freezing.

In short: movement prevents freezing.

Note: This works best with cold water. Hot water would have a higher temperature, so it would freeze less easily — but that’s not what you’re asking about. You’re asking about the dripping faucet, which is why it worked.

(If you have a water heater or a hot water system, the hot water might not freeze at all — but that’s a different story.)
